history.name: Apollo 1
history.what: During a launch-pad test with the cabin full of pure oxygen, a fire swept through the command module in seconds. The three astronauts died from carbon monoxide and toxic gases before the hatch could be opened.

quotes.text: Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly, causing a rapid rise in temperature and pressure that led to the rupture of the Command Module pressure vessel.
U.S. Air Force pathologists concluded the astronauts perished from asphyxia from carbon monoxide and other toxic gases resulting from the fire. Their burns were likely survivable.
100% oxygen at 16.2 psi (the conditions that were present during the Apollo fire)

history.changed: NASA restricted the amount and location of combustible material, redesigned the hatch to open in three seconds and made spacesuits from fire-resistant materials.

changed_quote.text: NASA restricted and controlled the amount and location of combustible material within the spacecraft.

history.today: The launch-pad fire shows why cabin pressure, oxygen fraction, material selection and escape provisions must be considered together. The later flight measurements shown here cover different materials and test conditions.

history.name: Apollo flammability tests
history.what: NASA made 102 deliberate ignitions in a command-module mock-up at three combinations of oxygen and pressure. The tests examined the modified cabin after the Apollo 1 fire.

quotes.text: Engineers in Houston conducted three series of tests comprising 102 deliberate ignitions between December 1967 and February 1968 at varying cabin atmospheric composition and pressure
Many of the fires self-extinguished during testing and all could have been dealt with easily by onboard firefighting equipment.

history.changed: The tests set the cabin atmospheres for ground testing, prelaunch and flight.

changed_quote.text: The series of tests led to a determination of ideal cabin atmospheres during ground testing, prelaunch operations and flight.

history.today: The distinction between a tested material and an entire cabin also matters for exploration. Saffire-VI provides flight measurements on particular materials at reduced pressure and elevated oxygen.

history.name: Apollo 13
history.what: An oxygen-tank heater and its thermostat were incompatible with the voltage used during a ground test. The heater overheated and damaged wire insulation. The tank exploded during the flight. The crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat and returned to Earth.

quotes.text: During the final test on the launch pad, the heaters were left on for an extended period and reached temperatures around 1000 degrees Fahrenheit, degrading the Teflon insulation.

history.changed: The oxygen tank system was redesigned: a third tank in another bay, better thermostats, no stirring fans, and all wiring sheathed in stainless steel.

changed_quote.text: redesigned the oxygen tank system by adding a third tank in a different bay, upgrading thermostats, removing stirring fans and sheathing all electrical wiring in stainless steel.

history.today: The damaged insulation was inside an oxygen tank. Cabin flame-spread experiments address a different environment and cannot quantify the risk of a fault in oxygen-system wiring.

history.name: Fire on Mir
history.what: A solid-fuel oxygen generator burst into flames on the Mir space station, blocking the way to one of the two Soyuz escape craft and filling the modules with dense smoke. The crew put on masks and fought it with three extinguishers.

quotes.text: the canister ignited, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke.
The flame finally extinguished itself, with Korzun’s efforts preventing significant damage
Over the next several hours, the station’s life support system cleared the smoke

history.changed: Russia changed crew training and ground response, and the canister preparation. The ISS uses electrolysis as its main oxygen source, with improved solid-fuel generators as backup.

changed_quote.text: They identified the most likely culprit as latex working glove material inadvertently introduced into the canister.

history.today: The fire blocked an escape route for minutes, and clearing the smoke took hours. SAME and SAME-R measured smoke from overheated materials aboard the ISS. Their published condition tables omit ambient oxygen and pressure.

spinoffs.name: Lighter firefighter air tanks
spinoffs.what: Scott Aviation and NASA Johnson developed a composite air-tank backpack weighing 20 pounds for a 30-minute air supply. It was 13 pounds lighter than the conventional equipment described in 1976.
spinoffs.quote: New backpack system weighs only 20 pounds for 30 minute air supply, 13 pounds less than conventional firefighting tanks.

spinoffs.name: Fewer false fire alarms
spinoffs.what: The Shuttle detector distinguished combustion particles from dust, reducing susceptibility to false alarms. NASA described networks of these sensors as a possible way to monitor large spaces such as mines.
spinoffs.quote: can discriminate between combustion particles and extraneous matters such as dust. This gives an important advantage; it is less susceptible to false alarms.

spinoffs.name: Fire-resistant gear
spinoffs.what: NASA and the U.S. Fire Administration evaluated heat-protective materials derived from spacesuits and spacecraft components for firefighter clothing. Fourteen municipal fire departments participated in the field evaluation.
spinoffs.quote: A major focus of the effort involves application to the FIRES ensemble of lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials originally developed for use in astronauts' space suits or in spacecraft components which require thermal protection.

not_conservative.text: Recent results from the BASS experiment currently running on the ISS indicate that NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is not conservative, and materials can burn at lower oxygen levels in microgravity than on Earth.

local_jet.text: Also, current findings show that local application of suppressant is not adequate for flame extinguishment. The local jet entrains air and sustains the flame even when the ambient airflow is turned off.

ventilation_speed.text: the characteristic gas velocity of the minimum in the curve is on the order of 10 cm/s and also corresponds to a maximum in the flame spread rate. To give perspective, this is the velocity typical of that of spacecraft ventilation systems.

upstream.text: Completely contrary to normal-gravity behavior, the flame spreads upstream, into the oncoming airflow, in space when the forced-flow velocities are low

sofie_sea.text: SoFIE can accommodate testing in exploration atmospheres with reduced pressure and elevated oxygen

ext_velocity_21.text: When tests are repeated with samples of different thicknesses, the extinction velocities are found to be about 1 cm/s for 100, 200, and 300 μm and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 μm.

ext_velocity_16.text: the extinction velocities were found to be about 2.6 cm/s for 100 μm and about 4 cm/s for 200 μm

PSI-10.text: Flame Design studied soot formation in spherical diffusion flames. Its normal-flame table lists ethylene and propane in oxygen-containing chamber atmospheres. Initial chamber oxygen reached 40 %, including 131 normal-flame runs at 30 % or higher.

PSI-20.text: A porous gas burner emulated a burning solid. The investigators proposed three cabin atmospheres and reported that some flames persisted without forced airflow at elevated oxygen. At 21 % oxygen comparable flames extinguished shortly after the flow stopped. The results are preliminary. The day summaries omit pressure.

PSI-21.text: Weak methane and ethylene jet flames in a slow surrounding flow, measuring flame shape, lift-off, extinction limits and soot. Data for testing combustion models.

PSI-22.text: How an electric field changes a flame and its soot. The record says it does not serve space applications directly.

PSI-23.text: Gas diffusion flames produced with hydrogen, methane and ethylene fuels supplied data on growth and extinction. The daily conditions include different oxygen levels and diluents.

PSI-25.text: BASS-II tested PMMA and other solid materials in a flow duct aboard the ISS. Initial oxygen in the imported table ranged from 13.6 to 22.2 %. The table records conditions and gas readings. Images, video and the investigators’ report document how individual samples burned.

PSI-26.text: The first BASS series: cotton-fiberglass fabric, PMMA, Nomex and Ultem burned in opposed and concurrent airflow, plus nitrogen as an extinguishing agent. The table lists only the sample material.

PSI-39.text: CFI examined cool-flame chemistry in dodecane droplets and fuel mixtures. Its table reports pressures from 0.5 to 5 atm. A droplet can continue reacting after its visible hot flame disappears.

PSI-47.text: Checked that a smoke particle counter works in weightlessness before it was used for the SAME smoke experiment.

PSI-60.text: A ground study that turned more than 1600 SPICE flame photographs into soot and temperature maps.

PSI-62.text: A ground modelling study of flame spread along a material in the direction of the airflow, compared with BASS flights. Aims at screening new materials on the computer.

PSI-68.text: FLEX-2 studied combustion of droplets of single fuels and mixtures. Its summary lists a test matrix spanning 17 to 30 % oxygen and 0.5 to 3 atm. Per-run oxygen, pressure and outcomes cannot be recovered by crossing the listed settings.

PSI-69.text: Methanol and heptane droplets burned in many atmospheres to find when a flame cannot survive, and how well carbon dioxide and helium put it out. 274 runs with recorded outcomes, from 12 to 34 % oxygen.

PSI-98.text: A large cotton–fiberglass sheet burned inside an uncrewed Cygnus after it left the ISS. The table gives dimensions of 94 by 40.6 cm and lists ignition power, airflow and burn duration.

PSI-99.text: Nine sample entries compare orbital and normal-gravity results for silicone, cotton–fiberglass fabric, PMMA and Nomex. All four silicone entries record approximately zero orbital burn length. The entry combining PMMA and Nomex specifies that only the PMMA burned.

PSI-100.text: A repeat of the large fabric fire on Cygnus, in airflow of 30 cm/s in both directions along the sample.

PSI-101.text: A reflight of the smoke experiment with improved particle collection, so spacecraft smoke detectors can be tuned to smoke made in weightlessness.

PSI-102.text: Heated Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, lamp wick and dibutyl phthalate until they smoked, and measured the particles. Tests whether weightless smoke particles are larger than on Earth.

PSI-106.text: Jet flames of methane, ethane and ethylene diluted with nitrogen, studied at the point where they lift off the burner. Flame stability data.

PSI-107.text: SPICE varied jet fuel flow and measured smoke-point behavior in coflowing air. The imported table contains 469 entries, including measurements at different fuel flow settings within a single flame-on interval.

PSI-115.text: Computer simulations of how smoke particles grow with and without gravity, built on the SAME data, to design better smoke detectors.

PSI-117.text: Computer study using FLEX flight data to explain why cool flames on droplets behaved differently from run to run.

PSI-142.text: Ground experiments and simulations that map when cool flames survive or go out, based on FLEX observations.

PSI-159.text: CFI-G studied ethane, propane and butane in normal and inverse spherical flames. The normal-flame table records oxygen in the ambient chamber. In the inverse-flame table, 12 to 85 % oxygen refers to the mixture delivered by the burner into a fuel-containing chamber.

data_notes: The PSI catalogue lists the ISS for Saffire-I and Saffire-III. NASA describes both flight experiments aboard uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft after departure from the station. Saffire-I’s catalogue dates also match those of SAME. Use the mission history for flight chronology.

task.text: Your challenge is to build an SI-powered, web-based dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets combustion science investigations to deliver critical foundational insights for fire safety.

obj_relevant.text: Identify investigations most relevant to the fire safety needs of habitable crew environments, including spacecraft, space stations, bases on the lunar and Martian surfaces, and pressurized rovers.

obj_data.text: Extract data that supports predictive modeling of flammability and fire scenarios in space exploration.

obj_controls.text: Highlight research that informs the development of next-generation fire safety controls and equipment.

pillars.text: NASA’s spacecraft fire safety work is focused on prevention, detection, and suppression.

prevention.text: Flammability studies focus on solid materials such as fabrics and plastics, as studied in the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) and Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) investigations.

detection.text: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

suppression.text: Suppression was studied in the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) through dilution of the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium, both of which suppress fire.

moon_air.text: The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less.

more_flammable.text: Compared to Earth’s atmosphere, that’s more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.

suit.text: To enable flexibility, spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen to only 4.3 psi (pounds per square inch), where the Earth’s pressure at sea level is 14.7 psi.

prebreathe.text: To reduce the pre-breathing duration and thus facilitate lunar excursions, it is expected that the Moon Base and pressurized rover(s) will be at a pressure and oxygen concentration between those in a spacesuit and the Earth’s atmosphere.

cfig.text: Microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were conducted as part of the ACME’s Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G).

cfig_85.text: an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame.

no_partial_g.text: there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI.

future_g.text: We expect such data will be added in the future, for example from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment.

efield.text: Partial gravity was mimicked in ACME’s Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment through the effect of the electric field on the ions that naturally occur in flames.

bound.text: Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what occurs at intermediate gravity levels.

bre.text: While it burned gaseous fuels, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project was a study of materials flammability in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.

daft.text: One of the instruments used for smoke detection in the SAME and SAME-R studies was instead used to detect dust in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2) studies.

others.text: Other combustion investigations within the PSI database (but not explicitly referenced above) are still relevant to fire safety, just not as strongly or directly.

hw_acme.text: The six experiments in the ACME project featured flames of gaseous fuels and were all conducted with the same modular set of ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

hw_mdca.text: FLEX, FLEX-2, and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) each featured burning droplets of liquid fuel and were conducted with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the CIR.

hw_msg.text: Each of these investigations was conducted within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the modular fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE.

earth.text: Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for use on the ISS have practical applications here on Earth, and NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection and firefighter gear, including protective clothing and air tanks.

scope.text: Fire safety involving rockets and propellants is generally beyond the scope of the research available in the PSI database.

audience.text: Your target audience can include professors, graduate students, undergraduate students, aerospace researchers, and aerospace engineers.

saffire6.text: this final iteration of the experiment was unique because of the higher oxygen concentration and lower pressure generated in the test unit to simulate the conditions within crewed spacecraft.

saffire6_materials.text: They then ignited a flame on materials such as plexiglass, cotton, Nomex, and Solid Inflammability Boundary at Low-Speed fabrics.

profiles._about: How each investigation is tied to fire safety. 'named' and 'related' follow the challenge statement word for word (see challenge_quotes); 'families' follow its Hardware section and the PSI hardware field; 'based_on' and 'fuel_class' follow each record's own title, objective and table. Scores built from these are judgements and are documented in the app.

external_saffire6.text: Saffire-VI flight events outside the imported PSI tables. Nomex did not ignite at 31.9 % oxygen. SIBAL cloth burned at 31.0 % and 54.1 kPa. Two-sided PMMA burned at 30.3 % and 54.6 kPa. One-sided PMMA burned at 28.8 % and 55.2 kPa. These pressures and oxygen fractions were recorded during the flight. The SIBAL and two-sided PMMA burns fall inside the dashboard exploration window. Table 1 gives no corresponding pressure for the Nomex event.

external_sofie.text: SoFIE-GEL flight tests on the ISS measured extinction of solid PMMA spheres in 13 to 34 % oxygen, at pressures from 0.15 to 1.1 atm and forced flows from 0.2 to 80 cm/s. The published ranges do not pair an oxygen concentration with a particular pressure. They cannot establish a run at the exact exploration atmosphere.
